title: White-Collar Crime Lawyer Cost: Fees, Phases and Who Pays (2026)
description: What white-collar criminal defense costs by phase, why document cases are expensive, and when an employer or insurer must advance your legal fees.
h1: How much does a white-collar crime lawyer cost?
summary: White-collar defense is usually billed hourly against an advance retainer, never on contingency, and costs are driven by document review, forensic accounting, parallel regulatory cases and whether the case goes to trial. Officers and directors may have their fees advanced by the company: Delaware law allows advancement if the person promises to repay fees if not entitled to indemnification. In federal court, people who cannot afford counsel can ask for a CJA lawyer, paid $177 per hour in 2026.
body:
What makes white-collar defense different

White-collar cases (fraud, embezzlement, bribery, tax, securities, health care and procurement fraud) are document cases. The prosecution's evidence is usually emails, spreadsheets, bank records and witness interviews collected over months or years. A defense lawyer's time goes into reading and organizing that record, finding the experts who can explain it, and, often, dealing with a parallel civil investigation by a regulator. That is why these cases cost more per charge than most street crimes, even when nobody goes to trial.

The stakes are real: in fiscal year 2025 there were 4,804 federal theft, property destruction and fraud cases; 75% of those sentenced went to prison, the average sentence was 23 months, and the median loss was $239,730 [1].

The phases that drive the bill

  • Pre-charge investigation. Responding to a subpoena, a search warrant or a target letter; advising on interviews; sometimes presenting the case to prosecutors to avoid charges. This is where good lawyering can change the outcome most, and where many matters end.
  • Document review and forensic accounting. Large productions need review software and staff time. A forensic accountant may be needed to rebut a loss figure, which also matters at sentencing.
  • Plea negotiation and sentencing. In federal cases the loss amount drives the Sentencing Guidelines range, so fighting the loss calculation is often the most valuable work.
  • Trial. Multi-week document trials require several lawyers and paralegals, which multiplies hourly costs.
  • Parallel proceedings. An SEC, IRS, state attorney general or licensing-board matter may need its own lawyer time, and what you say in one can be used in the other.

Example (illustrative, not a quote): a pre-charge matter that a lawyer resolves in 40 hours at the $349 national average rate [3] costs 40 × $349 = $13,960. A case that goes through a three-week trial with two lawyers billing 500 hours each costs 1,000 × $349 = $349,000 in lawyer time alone, before experts and e-discovery vendors. White-collar specialists at large firms usually bill well above the national average, so get a written phase-by-phase budget.

Who pays: you, your employer or an insurer

Many white-collar defendants are current or former officers, directors or employees, and the company may be required or allowed to pay.

  • Advancement. Under Delaware law, which governs many U.S. corporations, a company may pay an officer's or director's legal fees before the case ends if the person signs an undertaking to repay them if it is later determined they are not entitled to indemnification [2]. Company bylaws often make advancement mandatory; check yours.
  • Indemnification. For criminal matters, Delaware lets a corporation indemnify a person who acted in good faith and had no reasonable cause to believe the conduct was unlawful; the power is permissive, not automatic [2].
  • D&O insurance. Directors and officers liability policies often cover defense costs for investigations, subject to limits, retentions and exclusions. Ask for the policy, not a summary.

When a company or insurer pays, the lawyer still works for you. California's Rule 1.8.6, for example, allows third-party payment only if it does not interfere with the lawyer's independent judgment, your confidential information is protected, and you give informed written consent [6]. Remember that the company's own lawyers represent the company, not you.

An undertaking to repay is a real debt. If you are convicted and the company determines you were not entitled to indemnification, it can demand the advanced fees back.

How white-collar lawyers structure fees

Most white-collar lawyers bill hourly against an advance retainer that sits in a client trust account and is drawn down as work is done [5]. Some quote flat fees for defined phases, such as responding to a subpoena. Contingent fees are prohibited in criminal defense under ABA Model Rule 1.5(d)(2) [4], and Rule 1.5(a) requires fees to be reasonable [4].

If you cannot afford private counsel once charged in federal court, you can ask for a court-appointed lawyer. CJA panel lawyers are paid $177 per hour in non-capital cases for work on or after January 1, 2026 [7]. See federal criminal defense lawyer cost for eligibility.

Questions to ask at the consultation

  • Have you handled this type of investigation with this agency and U.S. Attorney's office?
  • What is the budget for each phase, and who on your team will do the work at what rate?
  • Do you expect to need a forensic accountant or e-discovery vendor, and who hires them?
  • Will you coordinate with my company's counsel and insurer about advancement?
  • How will a parallel civil or regulatory case be staffed and billed?

When to call a lawyer

Call before you talk to investigators, as soon as you receive a subpoena, target letter or search warrant, or when your employer starts an internal investigation that involves you. Early advice is far cheaper than repairing a damaging interview later. For state-level charges, see criminal defense lawyer cost; for a general approach to comparing quotes, see how much does a lawyer cost.

faq.q: Will my company pay for my white-collar defense lawyer?
faq.a: Possibly. Many corporate bylaws and indemnification agreements require advancement of legal fees to officers and directors, and Delaware law permits it if you sign an undertaking to repay. Employees below officer level may or may not be covered, so ask for the bylaws, any indemnification agreement and the D&O policy.

faq.q: Can the company lawyer represent me too?
faq.a: The company’s lawyers represent the company. Their interests can diverge from yours, especially if the company is cooperating with prosecutors. Most people under investigation need their own lawyer.

faq.q: Why do white-collar lawyers need such large retainers?
faq.a: Because the work is front-loaded: reviewing documents, interviewing witnesses and retaining experts can start the day they are hired. The retainer is held in trust and drawn down as work is done, with unused funds normally returned.

faq.q: Is it worth hiring a lawyer before I am charged?
faq.a: Often yes. The pre-charge stage is when a lawyer can present information to prosecutors, prepare you for or advise against interviews, and sometimes avoid charges. It is usually much cheaper than defending an indictment.
